t.3.45.1: Then Vaidehī, questioned by Rāvaṇa, who wished to carry her off and had taken the form of a wandering ascetic, told of herself in her own words.
t.3.45.2: "He is a brāhmaṇa and a guest; if left unanswered, he would surely curse me." Having reflected thus for a moment, Sītā spoke these words.
t.3.45.3: I am the daughter of Janaka, the great-souled lord of Mithilā; Sītā is my name, and I am the wife of Rāma. May good fortune be yours, O best of the twice-born.
t.3.45.4: For a year I dwelt in Rāghava's house, enjoying human pleasures, with every desire fulfilled.
t.3.45.5: Then, after a year had passed, the king, together with the royal ministers, resolved to consecrate my husband Rāma.
t.3.45.6: But while preparations were being made for that consecration of Rāghava, my revered lady named Kaikeyī asked her husband for a boon.
t.3.45.7: But Kaikeyī, having laid claim upon my father-in-law by virtue of a good deed, asked her husband, that best of kings, true to his word, for two things: the banishment of my husband and the consecration of Bharata.
t.3.45.8: Today I shall not eat, nor shall I sleep, nor shall I ever drink; if Rāma is consecrated, this is the end of my life.
t.3.45.9: As Kaikeyī spoke thus, my father-in-law, that bestower of honour, pleaded with her, offering fitting inducements, but she would not grant his plea.
t.3.45.10: My husband, of great splendour, is twenty-five years of age; he is famed in the world as Rāma, virtuous, truthful in speech and pure, large-eyed and mighty-armed, devoted to the welfare of all beings.
t.3.45.11: But when Rāma, my husband, had come into his father's presence for the consecration, Kaikeyī hastily spoke these words to him.
t.3.45.12: Hear from me, O Rāghava, what has been commanded by your father: this kingdom, free of thorns, is to be given to Bharata.
t.3.45.13: But you indeed must dwell in the forest for nine years and five. Go forth into exile, O Kākutstha, and free your father from falsehood.
t.3.45.14: "So be it," said Rāma, who fears nothing from any quarter, to Kaikeyī; and my husband, firm in his vows, did as she had said.
t.3.45.15: He would give, but never receive; he would speak the truth, and never falsehood. This, O brahmin, is Rāma's firm and unsurpassed vow.
t.3.45.16: His half-brother, born of a different mother, is the mighty Lakṣmaṇa by name, a tiger among men, Rāma's companion in battle and a slayer of foes.
t.3.45.17: That brother of his, named Lakṣmaṇa, righteous in conduct and firm in his vows, followed him, bow in hand, as he went forth into exile together with me.
t.3.45.19: Rest and be at ease for a moment; you may stay here. My husband will soon return, bringing an abundance of forest fare.
t.3.45.18: Thus we three, cast out of the kingdom for Kaikeyī's sake, must roam, O best of the twice-born, through the deep forest by our own strength.
t.3.45.21: When Sītā, the wife of Rāma, spoke thus, the mighty Rāvaṇa, lord of the Rākṣasas, gave a fierce reply.
t.3.45.20: So tell me truly your name, your lineage and your family, and for what purpose, O twice-born one, do you wander alone in the Daṇḍaka forest?
t.3.45.22: O Sītā, I am that Rāvaṇa by name, lord of the hosts of Rākṣasas, by whom the worlds, together with the gods, Asuras and serpents, have been terrified.
t.3.45.23: But having seen you, gold-hued and clad in silk, O faultless lady, I find no delight in my own wives.
t.3.45.24: Of the many excellent women brought here from everywhere, of all of them, be my chief queen; blessings be upon you!
t.3.45.25: In the midst of the ocean lies my great city named Laṅkā, encircled by the sea and set upon the summit of a mountain.
t.3.45.27: Five thousand maidservants, adorned with every kind of ornament, will wait upon you, Sītā, if you become my wife.
t.3.45.26: There, O Sītā, you will roam with me through the forests, and you will no longer long for this life of dwelling in the wilderness, O beautiful lady.
t.3.45.28: Thus addressed by Rāvaṇa, the daughter of Janaka, flawless of limb, grew angry and replied, paying no regard to that rākṣasa.
t.3.45.29: I am devoted to Rāma, my husband, who is unshakable like a great mountain, equal to great Indra, and imperturbable like the great ocean.
t.3.45.30: I am devoted to Rāma, the mighty-armed, broad-chested one who moves with the stride of a lion, a lion among men, lion-like in form.
t.3.45.31: I am devoted to Rāma, whose face is like the full moon, the hero, the darling son of a king, master of his senses, of wide renown and mighty-armed.
t.3.45.32: But you, a jackal, desire me here, a lioness hard to attain. I cannot be touched by you, just as the radiance of the sun cannot be touched.
t.3.45.33: Surely, O wretched one, you are seeing many golden trees, you who desire the beloved wife of Rāghava, O Rāvaṇa!
t.3.45.34: You wish to pluck a fang from the mouth of a hungry and swift lion, the enemy of deer, and from the mouth of a venomous serpent.
t.3.45.35: You wish to carry off with your hand Mandara, the foremost of mountains; having drunk the Kālakūṭa poison, you wish to go away unharmed.
t.3.45.36: You are wiping your eye with a needle and licking a razor with your tongue, you who wish to possess Rāghava's beloved wife!
t.3.45.37: Having tied a stone around your neck, you wish to cross the ocean; you wish to seize both the sun and the moon with your two hands, you who wish to violate the beloved wife of Rāma.
t.3.45.38: You who wish to carry off Rāma's wife, whose conduct is virtuous, are one who, having seen a blazing fire, wishes to carry it away in a cloth.
t.3.45.39: You who wish to obtain the worthy wife of Rāma wish to walk upon the tips of iron-tipped spears.
t.3.45.40: Whatever difference there is between a lion and a jackal in the forest, whatever difference between a trickling stream and the ocean, whatever difference between the finest wine and sour gruel, that is the difference between Dāśarathi and you.
t.3.45.41: The difference between gold and lead, the difference between sandal-scented water and mire, the difference between an elephant and a cat in the forest, that very difference lies between Dāśarathi and you.
t.3.45.42: The difference that exists between a crow and Vainateya, the difference between a diver-bird and a peacock, the difference between a sārasa crane and a vulture in the forest, that same difference lies between Dāśarathi and you.
t.3.45.43: While Rāma, whose might equals that of the thousand-eyed Indra, stands with bow and arrows in hand, even if I am carried off by you I shall not be digested, just as a diamond swallowed by a fly is not.
t.3.45.44: Having thus spoken those well-considered words to that night-roamer, she of guileless heart grew distressed, trembling in every limb, like a slender plantain tree tossed by the wind.
t.3.45.45: Noticing Sītā trembling, that Rāvaṇa, whose might was equal to Death's, recounted his own lineage, strength, name and deeds in order to inspire fear.
